population.method_label: City's total, shared by actual growth
population.method_about: All of Calgary adds up to the City's own population estimate and forecast for that month, but growth is not spread evenly: each community is its 2021 Census count times one factor, plus the growth the growth model measured there (homes built since 2021). The factor spreads only what homes do not explain (more people per home since 2021, people in seniors' homes, residences and shelters, the Census undercount) over every community's 2021 count. Fast-building areas get their real growth; built-out ones grow less.

rezoning.note: Rezoning (land use redesignation) applications, numbered LOC: a change to what a property may be used for, decided by Council at a public hearing. Hearing dates are on Council agendas, not in the open data.

roadwork.title: Country Hills Boulevard NE Widening Project
roadwork.what: This project will widen the section of Country Hills Blvd between Barlow Trail and 36 Street N.E. to help reduce traffic, improve safety, and support future growth.

projects.title: Northeast Athletic Complex
projects.budget: $170.4 million, fully funded (2026 budget, approved December 2025)
projects.address: Northwest corner of 80 Avenue NE and Metis Trail NE (34.6-acre site)
projects.what: Calgary's first competition-capable cricket field, four outdoor multi-use artificial turf fields, an indoor fieldhouse with an artificial turf field and indoor cricket batting nets, 16 team rooms, spectator seating, pathways, picnic areas and a playground, on a 35-acre site. More than 500 parking spaces. General contractor: Ledcor. Development permit approved by Calgary Planning Commission on April 30, 2026.

projects.title: Blue Line LRT extension to 88 Avenue NE
projects.status: Design (30% design due about end of 2026)
projects.budget: About $160 million (estimate). Design funded by the City and Alberta; Alberta announced $43.3M toward construction in 2024; the rest is not yet secured
projects.completion: Construction tentatively 2028 (2027 if other governments fund it sooner)
projects.address: Saddletowne Station to a new station at 88 Avenue NE and 60 Street NE (about 1 km)
projects.what: One new station serving Savanna and nearby communities, an interim end point for local bus routes and the starting point for a future airport connection. Extending on to Country Hills Boulevard (for Cityscape, Redstone and Cornerstone) is in the 10-year capital plan but unfunded. In the City's 2026 engagement nearly 90% of 724 respondents supported it; parking, safety and lighting were the main concerns.

projects.title: New high school in Cornerstone (Calgary Board of Education)
projects.owner: Alberta Infrastructure for the Calgary School Division
projects.what: Grades 10 to 12, 2,410 students. Architect: Stantec. Announced with a K-4 school in Redstone; together they will serve over 3,000 students.

projects.title: New grades 5 to 9 school in Saddle Ridge (Calgary Board of Education)
projects.owner: Alberta Infrastructure for the Calgary School Division

projects.title: New K-4 elementary school in Redstone (Calgary Board of Education)
projects.owner: Alberta Infrastructure for the Calgary School Division
projects.what: Kindergarten to grade 4. Announced in 2025 with the Cornerstone high school.

projects.title: New Catholic elementary school in Redstone (Calgary Catholic School District)
projects.owner: Alberta Infrastructure for the Calgary Catholic School District
projects.status: Sod turned June 12, 2026; construction to follow
projects.what: Kindergarten to grade 6, 340 students. Not yet named.

projects.title: New schools in Cityscape (public elementary; Catholic elementary and junior high)
projects.owner: Calgary School Division and Calgary Catholic School District
projects.status: In Alberta's 2026 school capital list: public elementary in planning, Catholic elementary/junior high in design
projects.what: Two schools listed for Cityscape in Budget 2026.

projects.title: Lufthansa Technik engine maintenance facility (YYC AeroNex)
projects.owner: Calgary Airport Authority with Lufthansa Technik Canada
projects.what: About 150,000 sq. ft. engine repair shop with a test cell for Boeing 737 MAX engines; at least 160 permanent jobs by 2030 and 170 construction jobs. Part of the YYC AeroNex aviation hub.

projects.title: Saddle Ridge Crossing (condos, shops and offices)
projects.status: Phase one under construction (building permit for an office/retail building issued August 12, 2026)
projects.completion: 2026 to 2027 for phase one; more phases later
projects.what: Over 600 condos and about 200,000 sq. ft. of shops, restaurants, medical and other offices at full build-out. Phase one: 120 condos in two six-storey buildings and about 83,000 sq. ft. of commercial space.

access.revision: Revised 5 November 2026. This tab first counted amenities inside each community's boundary per resident. It now measures the distance from every home to the nearest amenity, in any community, and how many children or residents share the playgrounds and parks within reach. The earlier list of 23 communities is replaced.

playground.label: Playground
playground.title: Playground Equipment
playground.where: type_description='MULTI PLAY COMPLEX' AND life_cycle_status in('ACTIVE','INSTALLED')
playground.basis: A choice, not a standard: 400 m is about a five-minute walk and 800 m about ten minutes, common neighbourhood planning distances.
playground.limits: City-maintained play structures only (multi-play complexes that are active or installed); school, developer and condominium playgrounds that are not in the City's inventory are not counted.

park.label: Public park
park.title: Parks Sites

crowding_spec.unit: park hectares per 1,000 residents within reach

park.basis: A choice, not a standard: distance to the park's edge, 400 m and 800 m.
park.limits: Every City park site of any size counts, including small sub-neighbourhood parks and linear parks along pathways. Parks in new communities may still be held by the developer and missing from the City's inventory.

transit_stop.label: Transit stop
transit_stop.title: Calgary Transit Stops

crowding_spec.unit: transit stops per 1,000 residents within reach

transit_stop.basis: 400 m: Calgary Transit Service Guidelines (May 2025) measure coverage as a 400-metre distance from a bus stop, about a five-minute walk. 800 m is a choice, not from the guidelines.
transit_stop.limits: A stop is not a service level: how often buses come is not measured here.

community_centre.label: Community centre
community_centre.title: Community Services

crowding_spec.unit: community centres per 100,000 residents within reach

community_centre.basis: A choice, not a standard: 800 m and 1.6 km.
community_centre.limits: Community association halls and centres as the City lists them. Several large communities show no centre within 800 m, which may mean association halls are missing from the City's list: this figure needs checking. Opening hours and programs are not measured.

rec_centre.label: Indoor recreation centre
rec_centre.title: Recreation Facilities
rec_centre.where: facility_type in('Leisure Centre','Leisure Centre - Municipal','Aquatic & Fitness Centre','Fieldhouse')

crowding_spec.unit: indoor recreation centres per 100,000 residents within reach

rec_centre.basis: A choice, not a standard: 2 km and 5 km for facilities that serve several communities.
rec_centre.limits: Leisure centres, aquatic and fitness centres and fieldhouses, municipal and not-for-profit. Arenas, outdoor pools, golf courses and other single-purpose sites are left out. Capacity and opening hours are not measured.

library.label: Public library
library.title: Community Services
library.basis: A choice, not a standard: 2 km and 5 km.
library.limits: Library branches as the City lists them; hours and size are not measured.

limitations: Straight-line distance, not walking distance: walking routes are longer (curved streets, rivers, rail lines, major roads), so every share is the most generous reading.
The City's inventory only: school, developer, condominium, community association and private amenities are not counted.
A transit stop is not a service level: how often buses come is not measured.
The size and condition of amenities are not measured: each playground counts as one, whatever its size.
Park crowding counts each park's whole area, natural areas and regional parks included, so homes near a very large park (Nose Hill, Fish Creek) show very high hectares per 1,000 residents.
Rental units are partly estimated: purpose-built rental buildings count as their units, from building permits or, where no permit matches, estimated from assessed value.

Children and residents are spread evenly over the homes of each community, from the population model's estimates (the 2021 Census plus modelled growth), not counted. The crowding figures will be firmed up with the 2026 Census age data in 2027.
New communities on the city's edge are naturally farther from shared facilities (recreation centres, libraries), some planned for later phases.
Community centre data needs checking: several large communities show no community centre within 800 m, which may mean community association halls are missing from the City's list.

referendum.question: Question 1: Do you support the Government of Alberta taking increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities?

Question 2: Do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law mandating that only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status will be eligible for provincially-funded programs, such as health care, education and other social services?

Question 3: Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for social support programs as they do now, do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring all individuals with a non-permanent legal immigration status to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for any provincially-funded social support programs?

Question 4: Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for public health care and education as they do now, do you support the Government of Alberta charging a reasonable fee or premium to individuals with a non-permanent immigration status living in Alberta for their and their family's use of the health care and education systems?

Question 5: Do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring individuals to provide proof of citizenship, such as a passport, birth certificate or citizenship card, to vote in an Alberta provincial election?

Question 6: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to have provincial governments, and not the federal government, select the justices appointed to provincial King's Bench and Appeal courts?
Question 7: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to abolish the unelected federal Senate?

Question 8: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services, without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs?

Question 9: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to better protect provincial rights from federal interference by giving a province's laws dealing with provincial or shared areas of constitutional jurisdiction priority over federal laws when the province's laws and federal laws conflict?

Question 10: Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?

notes: Residents are counted with City's total, shared by actual growth (chosen in Settings): All of Calgary adds up to the City's own population estimate and forecast for that month, but growth is not spread evenly: each community is its 2021 Census count times one factor, plus the growth the growth model measured there (homes built since 2021). The factor spreads only what homes do not explain (more people per home since 2021, people in seniors' homes, residences and shelters, the Census undercount) over every community's 2021 count. Fast-building areas get their real growth; built-out ones grow less. The 2021 Census count is shown beside it. Rates per 1,000 residents a year use residents in the middle of each period.
Infrastructure reports are the 21 roads, water and sewer, and parks and trees service types used in the 311 equity study.
The City publishes most 311 requests at their community's centre point, not their address, so 311 is mapped by community, not by street.
Traffic incidents are the City's reported incidents with exact locations, inside the Ward 5 boundary.

Crime and disorder by community come from the Calgary Police Service community safety data (the data behind its Community Safety Dashboard), published every quarter by month. Incidents without a location are left out. The Crime Severity Index (Statistics Canada) compares Calgary with other cities each year.
